clinicalPearls: This is an overgrowth-with-intellectual-disability syndrome featuring tall stature, macrocephaly, and a recognisable facial appearance with heavy, straight eyebrows and narrow palpebral fissures
It is caused by heterozygous variants in DNMT3A, which encodes a DNA methyltransferase central to establishing DNA methylation patterns during development
Intellectual disability is usually mild to moderate, and behavioural features including autistic traits and psychiatric symptoms are frequently reported
Obesity and a tendency to a heavier build are common, and some individuals have joint hypermobility, scoliosis, or congenital heart anomalies

Because somatic DNMT3A variants are recurrent drivers in haematological malignancy, there is a recognised predisposition to acute myeloid leukaemia and other blood cancers, warranting clinical vigilance
Diagnosis is molecular, typically via exome or genome sequencing or an overgrowth/intellectual disability panel, after considering Sotos and Weaver syndromes
There is no disease-specific therapy; management is anticipatory and multidisciplinary with developmental support and awareness of the haematological risk
reference.pathophysiology: Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome is a chromatin-related overgrowth disorder caused by germline heterozygous variants in DNMT3A. This gene encodes a DNA methyltransferase responsible for de novo methylation of DNA, an epigenetic process that governs gene expression programmes during growth and neurodevelopment. Impaired DNMT3A function disturbs these methylation patterns, producing generalised overgrowth, macrocephaly, and neurodevelopmental features. Because the same gene is a recurrently mutated driver in myeloid malignancy at the somatic level, constitutional variants confer an increased lifetime risk of haematological cancers. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, and the majority of cases are de novo.
additionalDifferentials: Cohen syndrome and other obesity-associated intellectual disability syndromes
Other chromatin- or methylation-related overgrowth disorders
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing, or a targeted overgrowth/intellectual disability gene panel
Chromosomal microarray to exclude copy number abnormalities
Full blood count and clinical review with a low threshold for haematology referral given malignancy risk
Echocardiography if a congenital heart anomaly is suspected
redFlags: Unexplained cytopenias, easy bruising, recurrent infection, or constitutional symptoms suggesting haematological malignancy
Rapid neurological change or regression prompting re-evaluation
Progressive scoliosis with respiratory or neurological compromise
Symptoms of a significant congenital cardiac lesion
reference.prognosis: Many individuals have a relatively stable course determined mainly by their level of intellectual disability and associated features. The recognised predisposition to haematological malignancy is an important long-term consideration and should prompt prompt evaluation of suggestive symptoms, though most patients do not develop cancer.
pitfalls: Diagnosing Sotos syndrome clinically and failing to test DNMT3A
Overlooking the haematological malignancy predisposition when investigating cytopenias or constitutional symptoms
Attributing obesity and behavioural difficulties to unrelated causes rather than the underlying syndrome
Neglecting genetic counselling regarding the autosomal dominant, usually de novo, inheritance
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Provide developmental and educational support with early intervention and individualised learning plans for intellectual disability
Assess and manage behavioural and psychiatric features including autistic traits with appropriate therapy and psychiatric input
Maintain haematological vigilance for acute myeloid leukaemia and other blood cancers, with a low threshold for full blood count and haematology referral for suggestive symptoms
Support weight management to address the tendency to obesity
Screen for and manage scoliosis, joint hypermobility and any congenital cardiac anomaly with echocardiography and orthopaedic review as indicated
Coordinate care through clinical genetics and relevant paediatric and adult specialists
Offer genetic counselling, noting autosomal dominant inheritance with most cases arising de novo
